Because capillary potassium is always falsely elevated
quiz.why: Capillary specimens begin clotting within seconds and platelets clump rapidly, so blood gas then EDTA then other additives then serum is the sequence. Microtainers do contain the same additives, and the difference is not driven by contamination or potassium.

quiz.q: A 7-year-old is terrified of the upcoming draw. Which intervention is most likely to help, and what is its constraint?
choices: Oral sucrose, which works at any age
Supine restraint by two staff, which shortens the procedure
Telling him it will not hurt at all
Topical anesthetic cream, which needs roughly 30 to 60 minutes and must therefore be requested early
quiz.why: Topical anesthetics are effective but require substantial onset time, which is exactly why they get skipped when nobody asks early. Sucrose works in infants rather than school-age children, restraint worsens distress, and false promises destroy trust for every future procedure.

quiz.q: You palpate a forearm and feel a soft compressible tube that rebounds, with one small firm knot along its length. What should you do?
choices: Choose a straight segment and enter below the knot, which is a valve
Enter directly over the knot, which anchors the vein
Abandon the arm because the vein is thrombosed
Use the visible blue surface line instead
quiz.why: A discrete knot in an otherwise soft vein is a valve, which hurts and stops flow if punctured directly. A thrombosed vein feels hard along its whole course, and visible surface lines are often small tributaries that collapse under vacuum.

quiz.q: A dehydrated elderly patient has no palpable veins. The labs are not time critical. Which action is most likely to succeed?
choices: Slap the antecubital fossa firmly to raise a vein
Move directly to a foot vein
Warm the arm at 40 to 42 C for 3 to 5 minutes and let it hang below heart level
Leave the tourniquet on for four minutes while searching
quiz.why: Warming plus gravity is the highest-yield and most under-used combination for a collapsed venous system. Slapping causes bruising and hemolysis, foot veins usually require a provider order, and a prolonged tourniquet causes hemoconcentration that falsely raises potassium.

quiz.q: You miss a vein on the first pass. Which adjustment is acceptable?
choices: Withdraw slightly and redirect once along the vein's line
Probe laterally until you feel the vein
Advance deeper until you get flashback
Reinsert through the same puncture at a 45 degree angle
quiz.why: A single small redirect along the vein's course is reasonable, while lateral probing tears tissue, causes hematoma and hemolysis, and is the mechanism of most nerve injuries. Blind deep advancement risks arterial puncture.

quiz.q: A patient with years of dialysis and multiple prior admissions needs labs. What is the single most efficient first step?
choices: Apply a tourniquet and inspect both antecubital fossae
Request ultrasound-guided access immediately
Warm both arms for five minutes before looking
Ask the patient where people usually get them, which arm works, and which spot never works
quiz.why: Patients with long access histories know their own map better than a forty-second survey will reveal, and asking costs nothing. Inspection, warming and ultrasound all remain useful but come after the free information.

quiz.q: Which IV securement practice is correct?
choices: Wrap circumferential tape around the forearm to hold the hub firmly
Cover the site with gauze and tape so it stays clean and dark
Leave the tubing straight with no loop to avoid kinking
Use a transparent dressing so the site stays visible, anchor a loop of tubing, and label with date, time, gauge and initials
quiz.why: Visibility allows early detection of infiltration and an anchored loop puts traction on tape rather than on the catheter. Circumferential tape hides swelling and can act as a tourniquet, and an unanchored straight line transmits every pull to the catheter tip.

quiz.q: During an IV start, the catheter will not thread after flashback, and you begin to withdraw it. What must you not do?
choices: Re-advance the needle into the partially withdrawn catheter
Release the tourniquet before removing the needle
Apply pressure above the insertion site
Activate the safety device after removal
quiz.why: The needle bevel can shear the catheter that has slid back over it, sending a plastic fragment into the circulation and requiring a tourniquet, immediate notification and imaging. The other three actions are all correct practice.

quiz.q: A patient receiving a vasopressor through a peripheral line develops a swollen, pale, cool forearm. What is the correct action?
choices: Remove the catheter immediately and elevate the arm
Increase the flush rate to clear the catheter
Apply a warm compress and continue the infusion at a lower rate
Stop the infusion, leave the catheter in place, notify at once, and mark the borders of the affected area
quiz.why: A vasopressor is a vesicant, so this is extravasation and the catheter may be the route for aspiration or an antidote such as phentolamine. Removing it forfeits that, and flushing or continuing drives more drug into tissue that can become necrotic.

quiz.q: Which statement about drawing blood from an intravenous catheter is correct?
choices: It is preferred over venipuncture because it spares the patient a stick
It is acceptable at the moment of insertion before fluid runs, but never from a line that is currently infusing
It is acceptable at any time as long as the line is flushed first
It produces less hemolysis than a clean venipuncture
quiz.why: A draw at insertion, before any fluid, is accepted in most departments, while drawing from an infusing line dilutes the sample and produces results that get acted on. Line draws hemolyze more often than fresh venipuncture, not less.

quiz.q: Two culture sets are drawn. Set A grows Staphylococcus epidermidis at 60 hours and set B is sterile. Set A was drawn from a new IV at insertion. What is the most likely root cause?
choices: A true bloodstream infection requiring vancomycin
An incubator failure in the laboratory
Insufficient volume in set B
Contamination, most likely from the line draw
quiz.why: A skin organism in one of two sets growing late, from a catheter draw, is the classic contamination pattern and is exactly why paired sets exist. Staphylococcus aureus, gram-negative rods and Candida would be treated as real regardless.

quiz.q: Which step most directly reduces blood culture contamination?
choices: Using a larger needle gauge
Locating the vein before prepping, scrubbing 30 seconds, and allowing at least 30 seconds of drying without re-touching
Drawing three sets instead of two
Refrigerating the bottles before incubation
quiz.why: Antiseptic only works with friction and full drying time, and re-palpating prepped skin reintroduces flora, so the ninety seconds before puncture is where contamination is decided. Needle size does not affect contamination, extra sets do not fix technique, and culture bottles are never refrigerated.

quiz.q: A clinically septic patient has four negative culture bottles at five days. Each bottle received about 4 mL. What explains this best?
choices: The organism is resistant to the culture medium
The bottles were drawn from two separate sites
Underfilling, since volume is the strongest single predictor of recovering an organism
The septa were cleaned with alcohol
quiz.why: Bacteria circulate at low concentrations, so roughly halving the inoculum meaningfully cuts sensitivity and can produce a false negative. Two sites and clean septa are both correct technique, and culture broth supports essentially all common pathogens.

quiz.q: Which organism, if it grows from a blood culture, is almost never dismissed as a contaminant?
choices: Coagulase-negative staphylococcus
Corynebacterium species
Staphylococcus aureus
Cutibacterium acnes
quiz.why: Staphylococcus aureus in blood is treated as a true bloodstream infection essentially always, and it carries a high complication rate. The other three are common skin flora and are the usual contaminants on case review.

quiz.q: The lab rejects a CBC as clotted. Which root cause fits best?
choices: The tube was drawn after a light blue tube
A 21 G needle was used instead of a butterfly
The tube was filled slightly above the line
The tube was not inverted promptly, or filled slowly from a poor stick
quiz.why: EDTA has to mix with blood immediately, and a slow trickling fill lets the first blood clot before the tube is full. Order of draw affects contamination rather than clotting, and a 21 G needle is the adult standard.

quiz.q: A metabolic panel drawn three hours ago sat at room temperature before reaching the lab. Which pattern is expected?
choices: Potassium falsely low and glucose falsely high
Potassium falsely high and glucose falsely low
Both falsely low
Both unchanged, because gel tubes stop metabolism
quiz.why: Cells continue to leak potassium and consume glucose while the specimen sits, roughly 5 to 7 mg/dL of glucose per hour without fluoride. Gel separates cells only after centrifugation, which had not occurred.

quiz.q: You have a difficult stick and obtained only about 2 mL of blood, but four tests are ordered. What is the correct action?
choices: Call the lab and ask which test to prioritize with the available volume
Divide the blood among four tubes and send them all
Send the fullest tube and cancel the rest without telling anyone
Add saline to reach the fill lines
quiz.why: Underfilled tubes produce wrong results rather than partial ones, and the lab knows minimum volumes and can rank the orders with the clinician. Silently cancelling tests and diluting specimens both create dangerous outcomes.

quiz.q: A patient with no bruising or bleeding has a reported platelet count of 19,000, and the smear shows clumping. What is the likely explanation?
choices: True severe thrombocytopenia requiring urgent transfusion
A hemolyzed specimen
An expired lavender tube
EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia, requiring a citrate tube redraw
quiz.why: EDTA causes platelets to clump in a small number of patients, so the analyzer undercounts them in someone with normal platelets, and a citrate specimen resolves it. Hemolysis and expired tubes produce different laboratory flags.

quiz.q: An arterial blood gas syringe has a small air bubble that was not expelled before transport. How are the results affected?
choices: Oxygen falsely high, carbon dioxide falsely low
Oxygen falsely low, carbon dioxide falsely high
Only the pH is affected
No effect, since the syringe was capped
quiz.why: Room air contains far more oxygen and almost no carbon dioxide than blood, so gases equilibrate across the bubble in both directions. Capping traps the bubble rather than neutralizing it, and pH shifts secondarily to the carbon dioxide change.

quiz.q: A clinician performs a modified Allen test before a radial puncture and color returns in 4 seconds. What does this mean?
choices: The hand depends entirely on the radial artery
Adequate ulnar collateral flow is suggested, though the test's predictive evidence is weak
The test is invalid because return should take at least 20 seconds
The radial artery is occluded
quiz.why: Prompt return of color suggests the ulnar artery can supply the hand, and about 5 to 15 seconds is the usual acceptable window. The test is widely taught but poorly predictive of ischemic complications, which is why many institutions no longer require it.

quiz.q: Which specimen must be transported at 37 C?
choices: Ammonia
Cold agglutinins
Lactate
Bilirubin
quiz.why: Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins react at low temperature, so cooling the specimen destroys the finding being tested for. Ammonia and lactate go on ice, and bilirubin is protected from light.

quiz.q: A stat type and screen and an ammonia level are both ready to go to the lab at 0200 during a trauma. How should they travel?
choices: Both by pneumatic tube for speed
Both hand-walked: blood bank specimens and iced specimens generally do not go by tube
The ammonia by tube and the type and screen by hand
Both left at the desk for the next courier run
quiz.why: Tube systems hemolyze specimens and most hospitals exclude blood bank samples and anything on ice, and both of these are time-critical during a trauma. Leaving them at a desk adds delay to two specimens whose values change with time.

quiz.q: A glucometer fails quality control twice with a fresh control vial that is in date. What is correct?
choices: Use it for patients and note the failure in the log
Tag it out of service, notify the point-of-care coordinator, use a backup or the main lab, and document
Calibrate it against a patient sample of known value
Continue testing until the next scheduled control
quiz.why: A device that has not passed current control cannot produce a usable result, so it is removed from service and clearly marked. Patient specimens are never used as calibrators, and continuing to test generates numbers a clinician may act on.

quiz.q: Besides scheduled intervals, new lots and shipments, and maintenance, what should prompt an immediate control run?
choices: Any result that does not fit the patient in front of you
The start of a new operator's shift
Any critical result, regardless of plausibility
The device battery dropping below half
quiz.why: A result that contradicts the clinical picture is the signal that something in the measurement chain has failed, and it is a device question and a patient question at once. Shift changes, plausible critical values and battery level are not themselves evidence of measurement error.

quiz.q: Your point-of-care operator identification suddenly stops working on the i-STAT. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The device needs a new battery
The cartridge lot has expired
Your documented competency has lapsed and the operator lockout has engaged
The device is out of quality control range
quiz.why: Competency, commonly reassessed at six months and then annually, is enforced through operator lockouts so untrained users cannot generate results. Battery, cartridge and control problems produce their own distinct errors rather than rejecting a specific user.

quiz.q: A point-of-care potassium comes back critically high on a device with current passing controls. What is the correct handling?
choices: Recheck it on the same device and report only if it repeats
Report it at the next handoff since the device passed control
Notify the nurse immediately, document who and when, and expect a confirmatory specimen to the laboratory
Discard it as unreliable because point-of-care potassium is not diagnostic
quiz.why: Point-of-care critical values carry the same notification obligation as laboratory values, and confirmation is a standard follow-up rather than a reason to withhold the result. Delaying or discarding a critical value leaves a potentially lethal electrolyte untreated.

quiz.q: You notice the blood bank band number on the tube has two digits transposed. What is the correct action?
choices: Correct the number, initial the change, and send it
Call the blood bank with the correct number
Discard the specimen and redraw, because blood bank specimens are never relabeled
Send it and let the blood bank reconcile against the chart
quiz.why: Any discrepancy on a blood bank specimen means discard and redraw, because relabeling defeats the exact control that prevents wrong blood in tube. Verbal corrections and reconciliation both assume the blood came from the right patient, which is what the control exists to verify.

quiz.q: A patient with no historical blood type on file needs red cells. The blood bank asks for a second specimen. Why will two tubes drawn together not satisfy this?
choices: Because the second tube would be too old by the time it is tested
Because the antibody screen must be repeated 24 hours later
Because two tubes collected in one event share the same identification error if one occurred
Because the second tube must be a different color
quiz.why: The requirement is for an independent collection, since the risk being controlled is a single wrong-patient event that both tubes would carry. Age, screen timing and tube color are unrelated to the purpose of the second determination.

quiz.q: A trauma patient needs blood immediately and no type is on file. What happens?
choices: Transfusion waits for a full crossmatch
Group AB red cells are released, since AB is the universal donor
Uncrossmatched group O red cells are released on a signed provider form, and the type and screen specimen is still drawn as early as possible
Only plasma may be given until a crossmatch completes
quiz.why: Emergency release uses group O red cells with O negative generally reserved for females of childbearing potential, and the specimen is still collected so the patient can be switched to type-specific blood quickly. AB is the universal plasma donor, not the universal red cell donor.

quiz.q: Fifteen minutes into a unit of red cells, the patient develops back pain, fever and rigors. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Slow the infusion and recheck vitals in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, keep the line open with saline through new tubing, notify, and save the bag and tubing
Stop the transfusion and remove the intravenous line
Complete the unit quickly to shorten total exposure
quiz.why: Stopping the product while preserving venous access is the priority, and new tubing prevents pushing residual incompatible blood in. The bag and tubing are needed for investigation, and the clerical check is repeated first because identification error is the most common cause of a fatal reaction.

quiz.q: You sustain a hollow-bore needlestick with visible blood on the device from a source of unknown status. What is the correct immediate sequence?
choices: Wash with soap and water for at least 30 seconds, report immediately, and go to employee health or the ED per policy
Squeeze the site to bleed it, apply bleach, and report at the end of the shift
Apply alcohol and continue working, reporting only if symptoms develop
Draw your own baseline labs and wait for results before telling anyone
quiz.why: Washing is the recommended first step, and immediate reporting starts the clock on prophylaxis that works best within about two hours. Squeezing and caustics damage tissue without reducing transmission, and waiting for symptoms or self-testing wastes the treatment window.

quiz.q: The source patient's rapid HIV test is 45 minutes away and your exposure was deep with a blood-filled hollow-bore needle. What should happen with post-exposure prophylaxis?
choices: Wait for the source result to avoid unnecessary medication
Prophylaxis is not indicated for needlestick injuries
Start the first dose now and stop it if the source tests negative
Begin only if you develop a fever within 72 hours
quiz.why: Effectiveness falls with delay and the target is within about two hours, so a high-risk exposure is treated first and reassessed when results return. Percutaneous hollow-bore injuries with visible blood are the highest-risk category, and symptoms are far too late a trigger.

quiz.q: Which statement about hepatitis exposure after a needlestick is correct?
choices: Hepatitis C has an effective post-exposure prophylaxis regimen
A documented hepatitis B vaccine responder still requires immune globulin
Neither virus requires follow-up testing once baseline labs are drawn
Hepatitis B management depends on the exposed worker's vaccination and immunity status, with immune globulin and vaccine for the non-immune ideally within 24 hours
quiz.why: A documented responder generally needs nothing further, while a non-immune worker receives immune globulin plus vaccine ideally within 24 hours and at most 7 days. Hepatitis C has no prophylaxis or vaccine, and both viruses require scheduled follow-up testing.

scenarios.title: Six days old, jaundiced, and everyone wants blood
scenarios.intro: A 6-day-old girl is brought in for yellow skin and poor feeding. She was born at term, weighs `3.1 kg`, and the provider orders a total and direct bilirubin, a CBC, a blood type and direct antiglobulin test, a blood culture, and a point-of-care glucose. The mother is exhausted and anxious.

steps.prompt: Before you touch the baby, what is the most important planning step?

choices.text: Total the required volume against her blood volume of roughly 80 to 100 mL/kg and confirm minimum volumes with the lab.
choices.feedback: Correct. At 3.1 kg she holds roughly 250 to 310 mL. Every milliliter is a real fraction of that, and the whole list has to fit in one collection.

choices.text: Lay out the tubes in the venous order of draw and go in.
choices.feedback: Laying out tubes is right, but the venous order is not the capillary order, and volume planning comes first in a neonate.

choices.text: Start with the glucose since it is fastest, then decide about the rest.
choices.feedback: Piecemeal collection in a neonate means repeated sticks. Decide the whole list before the first puncture.

steps.prompt: The culture needs a venipuncture, and the rest can come from a heel stick. You start with the heel stick. What do you do first?

choices.text: Warm the heel for 3 to 5 minutes at about 40 to 42 C and give oral sucrose about 2 minutes before the puncture.
choices.feedback: Correct. Warming multiplies blood flow and sucrose has a real analgesic effect at this age. Both are done before, not during.

choices.text: Clean the posterior curve of the heel and puncture to 2.4 mm for good flow.
choices.feedback: The calcaneus sits close under the posterior curve, and a puncture to bone can cause osteomyelitis. Use the plantar surfaces and never exceed 2.0 mm.

choices.text: Puncture immediately and squeeze rhythmically to fill the microtainer quickly.
choices.feedback: Milking hemolyzes the sample and forces in tissue fluid. On a bilirubin and a CBC, that means a rejected specimen and a second stick.

choices.text: Clean with alcohol, puncture the lateral plantar surface, and collect.
choices.feedback: Site and antisepsis are right, but skipping the warming and the sucrose costs you flow and costs her comfort.

steps.prompt: Blood is flowing well. You have a microtainer for the CBC, one for chemistry and bilirubin, and the glucose strip. In what order do you collect?

choices.text: Lavender EDTA first, then the other additive tubes, then serum.
choices.feedback: Correct. The capillary order puts the hematology tube early because capillary blood clots fast and platelets clump within seconds. A blood gas, if ordered, would come before it.

choices.text: Serum first, then green, then lavender, following the venous order.
choices.feedback: That is the venous order, which is about additive carryover. In capillary collection the driver is clotting speed, so EDTA goes early.

choices.text: Fill the chemistry tube first because the bilirubin is the reason she is here.
choices.feedback: Understandable, but it will cost you a clotted CBC. The bilirubin tolerates being second; the platelet count does not.

steps.prompt: The heel stick is done. The blood culture still needs a venipuncture. The mother asks whether she can hold her.

choices.text: Yes, and encourage it: have her hold the baby skin to skin or feed her, and prep the site properly while she is calm.
choices.feedback: Correct. Skin-to-skin and feeding during the procedure both reduce pain response, and a calm baby means a cleaner stick.

choices.text: No, the mother must step out so you can restrain the baby properly.
choices.feedback: Restraint raises distress and offers nothing that comfort positioning does not. Parents present is standard for pediatric procedures.

choices.text: Yes, but skip the blood culture since she has already been stuck once.
choices.feedback: The culture is the reason a febrile or unwell neonate gets a workup at all. It does not get dropped for convenience.

steps.prompt: You are prepping for the culture. Your department stocks chlorhexidine-alcohol and povidone-iodine.

choices.text: Check policy on antiseptic for an infant this age, prep with the approved agent, and allow the full drying time before puncture.
choices.feedback: Correct. Many protocols restrict chlorhexidine in very young infants and use povidone-iodine instead, which needs roughly 2 minutes to dry. Either way, the drying time is not optional.

choices.text: Use chlorhexidine and stick after five seconds since the baby is getting upset.
choices.feedback: Wet antiseptic has not killed anything. This is the single most common root cause on a contamination review.

choices.text: Use alcohol alone, since the volume is small.
choices.feedback: Alcohol alone is a venipuncture prep, not a culture prep. A contaminated neonatal culture can mean days of intravenous antibiotics and a hospital stay.

scenarios.debrief: Three things separate a neonatal collection from an adult one. Volume is the first: a 3.1 kg newborn holds around 250 to 310 mL, so the entire test list is planned and confirmed with the lab before a single puncture, and a second stick to fix an avoidable error is a real harm rather than an inconvenience. Technique is the second: plantar surfaces only, never deeper than 2.0 mm, warm for three to five minutes, wipe the first drop, and never squeeze, because milking hemolyzes and adds tissue fluid to the exact analytes being measured. And the capillary order of draw inverts the venous logic. Venous order exists to stop additive carryover; capillary order exists because the blood is clotting in front of you, so the EDTA tube comes early and serum comes last. Comfort is not decoration here. Sucrose, warmth and a parent's arms produce a calmer baby, a cleaner stick, and a specimen the lab will run.

scenarios.title: Stat lactate on a patient with no veins
scenarios.intro: A sepsis alert is called on a 63-year-old man with metastatic colon cancer. He has had two years of chemotherapy, a fistula in his left arm from a previous dialysis course, and he tells you every nurse who has ever tried has failed on the first attempt. The nurse needs blood cultures and a lactate before antibiotics, which are being mixed now.

steps.prompt: You have about five minutes before the antibiotic is ready. Where do you start?

choices.text: Ask him where people usually get him, which arm works, and which spots never work, while you warm the right arm.
choices.feedback: Correct. Thirty seconds of the patient's own map plus warming the arm is the highest-yield opening move in a difficult access patient.

choices.text: Apply a tourniquet to the left arm and look for anything usable near the fistula.
choices.feedback: Never. A fistula arm is off limits for tourniquets and draws entirely. This is one of the few absolute rules in phlebotomy.

choices.text: Go straight to the dorsal hand with a 23 G butterfly.
choices.feedback: Possible later, but you have skipped the free information and the warming, and hand veins hemolyze more easily, which matters for a potassium on a septic patient.

choices.text: Tell the nurse to give the antibiotic and you will get cultures afterward.
choices.feedback: Cultures after the first dose often never identify the organism. This is the one step in the sepsis bundle a tech can personally ruin.

steps.prompt: He says the right forearm works and the antecubital never does. You warm the forearm for three minutes and find a soft springy vein running straight along the cephalic course.

choices.text: Prep for blood cultures first: locate and mark beside the site, then scrub 30 seconds and let it dry fully before touching anything.
choices.feedback: Correct. Cultures come first in the order of draw, and finding the vein before prepping is what stops you re-contaminating clean skin.

choices.text: Draw the lactate first since it is the time-sensitive number, then the cultures.
choices.feedback: Cultures are always first in the order of draw, and both can come off the same stick. Reordering risks contaminating a sterile bottle.

choices.text: Prep with a quick alcohol wipe to save time, since he is septic.
choices.feedback: A contaminated culture in a septic cancer patient buys him days of vancomycin and possibly a central line. The 30 seconds is the fastest thing you will do all shift.

steps.prompt: You get flashback with a 21 G butterfly and the vein is holding. You have culture bottles, a green tube for the point-of-care lactate, a gold tube and a lavender tube.

choices.text: Aerobic bottle first because the butterfly tubing holds air, then anaerobic, then the remaining tubes in order of draw.
choices.feedback: Correct. With a butterfly the tubing air goes into the bottle where air belongs. With a syringe the answer flips to anaerobic first.

choices.text: Anaerobic bottle first to protect the fragile anaerobes.
choices.feedback: That is the syringe rule. With a butterfly, the roughly 0.5 mL of tubing air would be pushed into the anaerobic bottle.

choices.text: Fill the lavender first since it is the smallest and the vein may not hold.
choices.feedback: EDTA first contaminates everything after it with potassium and binds calcium. On a septic patient you would be chasing a false critical potassium within the hour.

steps.prompt: The vein stops flowing after you fill the aerobic bottle to about 5 mL and the anaerobic to about 3 mL. You still need the lactate.

choices.text: Get the lactate tube from this stick if any flow remains, then tell the nurse the culture volumes were short and hand off for a second site.
choices.feedback: Correct. The lactate drives the bundle, and the short volumes must be reported because they lower the culture's sensitivity and the team needs to know.

choices.text: Say nothing about the volumes; the bottles look reasonably full.
choices.feedback: Volume is the strongest predictor of recovering an organism. A quietly underfilled set can produce a false negative in a genuinely bacteremic patient.

choices.text: Top off the bottles from the second site later and treat it as one set.
choices.feedback: A set is a set. Combining sites destroys the comparison that makes two sets interpretable.

choices.text: Abandon the stick and start fresh at another site for everything.
choices.feedback: Wasteful of a working vein and of time on a sepsis clock. Take what this site will still give you first.

steps.prompt: Your second attempt at another site fails. The antibiotic is ready and the nurse is waiting on the second culture set.

choices.text: Stop after two attempts, tell the nurse now, and ask for ultrasound-guided access so the second set and the antibiotic are not delayed further.
choices.feedback: Correct. Two attempts then hand off, and ultrasound-guided access is the intended escalation rather than a last resort.

choices.text: Try a third time in the dorsal hand, since you are close.
choices.feedback: Success rates fall with each additional attempt by the same person while pain and hematoma climb. The policy exists for exactly this moment.

choices.text: Tell the nurse to hold antibiotics until you find someone to draw the second set.
choices.feedback: Cultures before antibiotics is the rule when obtaining them does not meaningfully delay the drug. An indefinite hold on a hypotensive septic patient is not that.

scenarios.debrief: This case stacks three rules that all point the same way. The patient's own map plus warmth beats any device, and a fistula arm is never a candidate no matter how good the vein looks. The order of draw is not negotiable even under a sepsis clock: cultures first, then citrate, serum, heparin, EDTA, fluoride, because an EDTA carryover on this patient would produce a false critical potassium that someone would treat. And with a butterfly the aerobic bottle is inoculated first, because the tubing holds roughly 0.5 mL of air and air belongs in the aerobic bottle; with a syringe the answer flips. Two things get reported out loud rather than quietly absorbed: short culture volumes, because volume is the strongest predictor of growth, and your own two failed attempts, because escalation to ultrasound-guided access is the plan, not the admission of a failure.

scenarios.title: 0300, a moved arm, and a needle through a glove
scenarios.intro: It is `0300`. You are drawing a febrile, agitated 41-year-old with a documented history of injection drug use. He jerks his arm as you withdraw the needle, the safety device does not engage, and the needle catches the side of your left index finger through your glove. There is a drop of blood at the puncture.

steps.prompt: What do you do in the first ten seconds?

choices.text: Secure the sharp in the container, step back from the bedside, and go wash the site.
choices.feedback: Correct. An uncontrolled sharp in a room with an agitated patient is a second injury waiting to happen, and you cannot manage yours while holding it.

choices.text: Squeeze the finger hard to make it bleed out any contamination.
choices.feedback: Squeezing damages tissue and does not reduce transmission. It is one of the most persistent myths in the job.

choices.text: Finish the draw first so the patient does not need a second stick.
choices.feedback: Your exposure clock has started. The tubes can be redrawn by someone else; the two-hour window cannot be extended.

choices.text: Wash with soap and running water for at least 30 seconds, then cover the site.
choices.feedback: Correct and sufficient. Soap and water is the recommended first step for a percutaneous exposure.

choices.text: Pour bleach on the finger, then wash.
choices.feedback: Caustics injure tissue without reducing transmission risk and are specifically advised against.

choices.text: Wipe with an alcohol pad and return to the floor.
choices.feedback: Not adequate, and returning to the floor without reporting is the step that costs people the prophylaxis window.

steps.prompt: It is 0304. The department is busy, you are one of two techs, and you feel embarrassed about the stick.

choices.text: Tell the charge nurse immediately and follow the exposure policy to employee health or the ED.
choices.feedback: Correct. Reporting is the process working, not a disciplinary event, and the medication clock started at the injury.

choices.text: Wait until the shift ends at 0700 so you do not leave the floor short.
choices.feedback: Four hours is more than half the ideal prophylaxis window. Underreporting is common and this is exactly why it matters.

choices.text: Tell a coworker but not the charge nurse, and decide later.
choices.feedback: An informal mention starts nothing: no source testing, no prophylaxis, no sharps log entry, no workers compensation record.

choices.text: Report it but decline evaluation since the puncture was small.
choices.feedback: The report is right, but a hollow-bore device with visible blood is the high-risk category regardless of how the wound looks.

steps.prompt: In the ED as a patient, the provider characterizes the exposure: hollow-bore needle that had been in a vein, visible blood on the device, source with unknown status. The source's rapid HIV test will take about 45 minutes.

choices.text: Start the first dose of post-exposure prophylaxis now, with the plan to stop it if the source tests negative.
choices.feedback: Correct. Effectiveness falls with delay, the target is within about two hours, and a negative source result later is a reason to stop rather than a reason to have waited.

choices.text: Wait the 45 minutes for the source result to avoid unnecessary medication.
choices.feedback: That is 45 minutes of a roughly two-hour window spent on a decision that can be reversed in either direction later.

choices.text: Decline prophylaxis and plan to test yourself at six weeks.
choices.feedback: Testing is surveillance, not prevention. A high-risk percutaneous exposure is the scenario prophylaxis exists for.

steps.prompt: Your record shows a completed hepatitis B series with documented immunity. The provider reviews hepatitis planning and the incident paperwork.

choices.text: Expect no hepatitis B intervention given documented immunity, no hepatitis C prophylaxis but scheduled follow-up testing, and complete the sharps injury log with the device type and brand and how it happened.
choices.feedback: Correct on all three. The device detail on the log is how an unsafe product gets identified and replaced across the hospital.

choices.text: Expect hepatitis B immune globulin anyway, plus hepatitis C prophylaxis.
choices.feedback: A documented responder generally needs nothing further for hepatitis B, and there is no prophylaxis for hepatitis C at all, only testing and follow-up.

choices.text: Complete the incident report but skip the sharps log, since the device was a standard butterfly.
choices.feedback: The sharps injury log is a federal requirement and its whole purpose is capturing which devices are failing, including common ones.

scenarios.debrief: Everything in this case is a clock. Wash with soap and water, never squeeze and never use caustics. Report within minutes, because post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV works best started within about two hours and is generally not offered past 72 hours, and a significant exposure is treated before the source result returns rather than after. Hepatitis B is answered by your own vaccination record: a documented responder needs nothing further, while a non-immune worker gets immune globulin and vaccine ideally within 24 hours. Hepatitis C has no prophylaxis and no vaccine, only baseline and scheduled follow-up testing, which matters because acute hepatitis C is highly curable when it is found. The paperwork earns its place too: the federal sharps injury log records the device type and brand and how the injury happened, which is the mechanism by which a device that fails to engage under a moving patient gets replaced everywhere. And the root cause here was foreseeable. An agitated patient is a two-person draw.
